questiontext.text: In a sealed-bid second-price auction with private values, why is bidding your true value weakly dominant?

generalfeedback.text: Your bid determines only whether you win, never the price, which is the highest rival bid. Overbidding can only make you win at a price above your value; underbidding can only make you lose an auction you would have won at a profit. No beliefs about rivals are required.

answer.text: Your bid affects only whether you win, not what you pay, so misreporting can only cause bad wins or lost profitable wins
Bidding truthfully maximises the seller's revenue

feedback.text: Dominance is about your own payoff, not the seller's.

answer.text: All bidders have the same valuation
The auction is zero-sum

feedback.text: It is not, and the argument does not use this.

questiontext.text: Four risk-neutral bidders have values drawn independently and uniformly from [0, 1]. In the symmetric equilibrium of a first-price sealed-bid auction, what does a bidder with value 0.8 bid?

generalfeedback.text: The equilibrium bid function is \(b(v) = \dfrac{n-1}{n} v\). With \(n = 4\) that is \(0.75 \times 0.8 = 0.6\). As n grows the shading shrinks, because the risk of losing a profitable auction rises.

questiontext.text: Same setting: 4 bidders, values uniform on [0, 1]. What is the seller's expected revenue in any of the four standard auctions? Give a decimal.

generalfeedback.text: By revenue equivalence, expected revenue equals the expected second-highest value, which for \(n\) uniform draws is \(\dfrac{n-1}{n+1} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6\). Note that this coincides numerically with the previous answer only by construction of the example.

questiontext.text: Which pairing of auction formats is strategically equivalent under independent private values?

generalfeedback.text: The Dutch auction is equivalent to the first-price sealed-bid auction: in both, a bidder commits to a single number and pays it, learning nothing useful along the way. The English auction is equivalent to the second-price auction, because the winner effectively pays the point at which the last rival dropped out.

answer.text: Dutch and first-price sealed bid; English and second-price sealed bid
Dutch and second-price sealed bid; English and first-price sealed bid

feedback.text: The pairings are the other way round.

answer.text: All four are strategically identical

feedback.text: They yield equal expected revenue but call for different strategies.

answer.text: None are equivalent

questiontext.text: Revenue equivalence continues to hold when bidders are risk averse.

generalfeedback.text: False. With risk-averse bidders the first-price auction raises more, because bidders bid higher to reduce the risk of losing. Revenue equivalence also fails with asymmetric bidders, budget constraints, collusion and interdependent values - which is precisely why format choice matters in practice.

answer.text: true
false

questiontext.text: In a common-value auction, the winner's curse arises because:

generalfeedback.text: Winning selects the most optimistic estimate, so the fact of winning is itself evidence that your estimate was too high. Rational bidders correct for this by shading, and by shading more when there are more rivals. The phenomenon is documented in oil-lease and corporate-takeover data.

answer.text: The winner is the bidder with the most optimistic estimate, so winning is evidence of over-estimation
The winner always pays more than the second-highest bid

feedback.text: That is false in a second-price auction and not the mechanism of the curse.

answer.text: Bidders have different true values for the object

feedback.text: Common values means the true value is the same for all.

answer.text: The seller sets a reserve price above the true value

generalfeedback.text: Any outcome that some mechanism achieves in equilibrium can also be achieved by a direct mechanism in which agents report their types truthfully. This lets the designer restrict attention to truthful direct mechanisms without loss of generality, which is what makes mechanism design tractable.

answer.text: Any outcome achievable in equilibrium by some mechanism is achievable by a truthful direct mechanism
Truthful reporting is always a dominant strategy in every mechanism

feedback.text: Far from it; that is the property a designer must engineer.

answer.text: Every mechanism reveals the agents' types to the designer
Auctions always reveal the true value of the object

questiontext.text: The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem implies that with three or more outcomes, any deterministic, onto and strategy-proof voting rule must be a dictatorship.

generalfeedback.text: True. This impossibility result is why mechanism design so often introduces money (as in VCG), restricts preference domains (as in single-peaked preferences or matching markets), or settles for Bayesian rather than dominant-strategy incentive compatibility.

answer.text: true
false
